blocks.text: The lamplighter put his list on the Exchange Desk at dusk, four days after I lost my name.
Ordinary ink, on the back of a lamp-round sheet. Twelve numbered lines. Things he was sure of about himself.

"Six of these don't check," he said. "I've walked to every one. The places aren't there. And every one of them feels like mine." He pushed the sheet towards me. "I want to know which of my memories are mine."
Footnote: it was the first question anyone had ever asked me that I was qualified to answer.

His name was Josiah Teague. He lit the river round: the Tessary bridge, the Wharf Steps, a hundred and twelve lamps a night for eleven years. He had a lamplighter's hands, black at the fingertips, and he held his cap in both of them.
I am a trainee. Trainees do not take cases. I wrote his name in the day book, and the time, and told him to come back at ten in the morning, and he thanked me as if I had done something.
Behind me, Mr Gammage, the night clerk, was sorting the Weirside packets for the dawn opening. He didn't look up.
My mother called me Edric at supper. I answered.
The next morning Gideon Pask put a book on the kit-room counter. Grey board covers, thumb-sized, a brass clasp.

"Ballast Book, chick. Vesey's own, first printed thirty-one years ago. Thirty-one kinds." He hummed two bars of the tune nobody knows and tapped the cover. "That's all the kinds there are. Don't go inventing a thirty-second. Cleverer heads than yours have tried, and the Fan won't have it. A new design inside a kind is the same kind."
I opened it. Marked stone. Private knot. Coined word. Folded paper. Twenty-seven more, each with a page of designs and a page of warnings.

"Rules," said Gideon, and counted them on his fingers, which are thick and slow and never miscount. "One. You make it at home, with your hands. An act, not a thought. Two. It settles at the seventh midnight after you made it. Made, chick, not after you leave. Settles before any rent due that same midnight, so ballast never pays rent. Don't ever let anyone tell you different. Three. Anyone sees it or hears of it, it's spoiled. A witness is a support. Four. Once a branch has had a kind off you, that kind's dead there for good. Five." He held up his thumb. "It fails per counterpart, chick, not per traveller. Two of you with the one counterpart, you share the thirty-one."
"When would two travellers have the same counterpart?"
"Never seen it." He shrugged. "It's in the book."
Footnote: I could not think of a case. I filed the clause anyway.
Brisk came through with a coil of door-cord over her shoulder and signed for a lamp wick.
"Forty-one," she told Gideon, before he asked.
"You were twenty-nine five days ago, Brisk."
"Hard week."
I closed the book. "I'd like to practise. One ballasted crossing. Weirside. Today."
Cressida was in the doorway. I don't know how long she had been there. She is never early and never late, and apparently she is never not in doorways.
"To survey what?"
I had an answer prepared. It was about seal angles at the Weirside desk. It was a good answer. It was not the reason, and she knew it, and I knew she knew it.
"Grounded," she said. "A week."
"Under what clause, chief?"
"Under mine." She put the day book on the counter, open to last night's entry in my hand. "You have a desk. You have a lamplighter. Sallis is already at it."

Verity Sallis is top of the trainee cohort, and says so. She had taken the end of the Exchange Desk nearest the window, which is the end furthest from the doors. The desk stands in the threshold room. To reach it you have to pass the Ninefold's west door, and Verity went round its frame at an arm's length, the way you go round a sleeping dog.
Footnote: she has never touched a doorframe in my presence. I have watched.
"Ardent." She didn't look up. "Your lamplighter's received facts all fit one branch. I need his ages."
"You've had the list since eight?"

"Since seven. Gammage left it out." She turned her ruled sheet so I could read it. Verity's Least-Agreement Tables are a printed grid, five classes down the side, with ages across the top. She fills them in pencil and is right about four times in five, and says that too.
Josiah came at ten. He sat with his cap on his knee and answered her questions while she wrote. At the end she read it back to him, flat, like a tide table.

"Somebody is renting in the Bole and you are their counterpart. Each seventh midnight the Bole takes one fact from them and gives them your version. You get theirs. Least Agreement, in order. Class one, hinge: none. Class two, glare: none, or you'd be holding something the Bole can't make. Class three, ballast: settled, or you'd be losing nothing. Class four, orphans, the oldest first. Here's what you've received." She ran her pencil down. "At three: your father lifting you onto the parapet of the Low Bridge to watch the lamps lit. Five: letters learned at a dame school in Coldharbour Row. Six: lost an afternoon in the glassworks yard at Netherquay. Eight: learned to swim in the Netherquay basin. Nine: won the boys' race at the Candle Fair. Eleven: sold tapers from your mother's chandlery in Coldharbour Row."
"Those are mine," said Josiah. He didn't sound sure.

"They feel like yours. That's how it works. But the Bole has no Low Bridge, no Coldharbour Row, no glassworks at Netherquay and no Candle Fair. The Bole cut its hiring fair a century ago." Verity tapped the pin-card index. "One pinned branch has all four in its route. Lowbridge. Distance twenty-three."
"How often?" I said.
"Every seventh night." Josiah turned the cap round. "I wake when the bells strike twelve and something's gone. I don't know what. I just feel robbed."
"Six times," said Verity. "So the seventh is tomorrow night." She went on writing. "Next oldest. You were bound to the Lamp Office at thirteen?"
"Signed my indenture at the counter. My mother held the pen for me after."

"In Lowbridge boys are bound at the Candle Fair. It's the next thing in your life their route touches." She took out her bottle of pinned ink, which every trainee gets one of a quarter, and uncapped it, and wrote one line in the margin of her grid in a hand like engraving.
Teague, J., of the Bole: signed his indenture at the Lamp Office counter, aged thirteen; his mother held the pen after. Goes at the midnight ending day six.
"Seventy-eight percent," she said. "Sign there, Mr Teague. So we can both see it read false."
That evening I walked the river round with him, because it was his round and his case and I was grounded with nothing else to walk. Brisk came, because Brisk will come anywhere there's a ladder.
The Tessary bridge is high, stone, fourteen lamps a side. Josiah lit them from the pole with a little brass hook, and as each one caught, Brisk counted it out loud.

"Twelve. Thirteen. Fourteen." She leaned on the parapet, which is chest-high and no use for lifting a child onto. "First thing I remember in this life. Being carried over this bridge, counting these lamps. Somebody's arm under me. I got to fourteen and they said, good girl."
"Is that yours?" said Josiah.
"Far as I know." She grinned. "I've lost worse."
He looked down the river towards the narrows, where there is no Low Bridge and never has been.
"I've stood here every night for six weeks," he said, "looking for a bridge I remember being lifted onto. My father's hands. I can feel his thumbs under my arms. And it isn't there."
Footnote: you feel that something was taken, never what. Nobody had told him that what you get feels exactly as true. I hadn't known how to say it either, four days ago.
At the midnight ending day six, Verity and I sat in Josiah Teague's kitchen on Tallow Street with the grid on the table between the cups.
He had his cap on the table too. I don't know why. Maybe he wanted to keep his hands on something.
The bells began at the Wharf chapel. On the twelfth stroke he put his hand flat on the table and breathed out hard, the way you do when someone takes the chair out from under you.
"There," he said. "That's it. That's the feeling."
Verity turned the grid towards him and put her finger under the line in pinned ink.
He read it twice.

"That's wrong," he said slowly. "I was bound at the Candle Fair. In the square, in the snow, under the tallow-merchants' awning. I remember my boots." He looked at his own signature beside the line. "That's my hand."
"It is," said Verity.
"Then what's—" He stopped.
"It's what went," I said. "In your own hand. It won't feel true. Mine doesn't either."
Verity capped her ink. "Four in five," she said. "This was one of the four." It was the only time I have ever heard her say it quietly.
I did the arithmetic on the back of my own bill folder, because I could. Seven rents. Seven sevens. Forty-nine midnights back from tonight.
Footnote: rent is counted from arrival. So the grid doesn't just tell you what goes. It tells you when they came.

The Ninefold keeps a threshold log. Every opening, both sides, every name that comes through, in ordinary ink in a ledger the size of a tombstone. On the morning of day seven, Cressida turned it back forty-nine days for me with one finger.
Lowbridge side, dawn. One arrival.
Teague, A. Archive delegate, Lowbridge Survey. In.
There was no Out.
"Teague," I said. "Same surname. Different first name. His mother called him Amos." I paused. "Footnote, chief: I know something about that."
"Is that evidence?"
"No."
"Then find him."

We didn't, for four days. Brisk walked every lodging house on the south bank. Cressida would not spend an opening on a letter to Lowbridge until she had something to put in it. Verity said there was a sixty-one percent chance he had left the city. I sat at my desk, grounded, with the grid.
On the evening of day ten, I stopped looking at the grid and started looking at what Amos Teague had been given.

He had whatever Josiah's father had lifted him onto at three. He had Josiah's letters, wherever Josiah had learned them. He had six weeks of a Bole childhood in exchange for his own, and every one of those memories felt like home. And Josiah had grown up on the river and never left it.
Footnote: if you had lost your oldest memory and been handed another man's, and you were homesick, where would you go?

On day eleven, at lamp-lighting, Brisk and Cressida and I stood at the top of the Wharf Steps. Josiah came along the quay with his pole and lit the lamps, one at a time, down to the water. In the doorway of a shut chandlery across the street, a man in a long grey coat watched every one of them catch.
He had Josiah's jaw and Josiah's shoulders, and he looked like Josiah's older brother who had eaten better.
He didn't run. He was an archivist, not a surveyor, and I think he had been waiting for six weeks to be found.
"I made my ballast three days before I left," he said. We sat him on the steps. "To be safe. A six-day archive exchange. I counted from the day I left."
"Made, sir," I said. "Not left."

"I know that now." He rubbed his face. "It settled on my fourth night here. I found out on the fifth. An exit would be unballasted. And the first thing it would take is the oldest thing I have that the Bole doesn't. My father. On the steps. Lifting me up to see the lamps." He nodded down the steps at the water. "These steps."
Cressida said nothing. That is how she makes room.
"So you stayed," I said.
"Rent takes the small change. Everybody knows that."
"Everybody in Lowbridge," said Brisk.
I opened Verity's grid on my knee. I wasn't gentle about it. I didn't know how to be gentle yet.
"Where are the Wharf Steps in Lowbridge, Mr Teague?"
He opened his mouth. "At the—" He stopped. I watched him look for them in his own city and not find them.

"Rent follows Least Agreement like any swap. Same order. Oldest orphan first." I read him Josiah's line one. "'My father lifted me onto the parapet of the Low Bridge to watch the lamps lit.' That's yours. It went at your first rent, six weeks ago, three nights after your ballast had settled. The memory you've been hiding to protect is Josiah's."
He listened to it. He said, "There's a parapet. On the Low Bridge. I've walked it a thousand times." And then, quite reasonably: "I've never been lifted onto it."
Then he sat on his hands, the way Josiah had held his cap.

I counted it for him, because somebody had to say it in the order it happened. Seven rents. Seven facts out of a lamplighter on Tallow Street, none of them his to give. His father's hands at three. His letters at five. A lost afternoon at six, the swim at eight, the race at nine, the tapers at eleven, the indenture at thirteen. And seven out of Amos Teague. Forty-nine days. One fact a week, so that one memory could stay safe, and it had gone first.
Footnote: I'd like to say I felt sorry for him first. I felt sorry for Josiah first. I've since corrected the order.
On day twelve Josiah Teague sat in Cressida's office with his cap on his knee and asked whether he could have them back.
Cressida answered him properly, which with her means one sentence per fact.

"A rent swap is charged to the threshold the renter last came through. His is the Ninefold's north door, Lowbridge. It can be settled only there. Both of you, one on each side, hands clasped across an opening. Both consenting freely. Each fact named from pinned ink. Not before it has set thirty days." She paused. "Nothing of yours was written down."
"One line was," I said.
Verity, who had come in without being asked, put the grid on the desk. One line in pinned ink, in her engraver's hand, signed Teague, J.
Cressida looked at it for a long moment. "Then one," she said. "In thirty days. At that door. With him on his own side."
Josiah looked at the line as if it were a ticket.

Amos was in the kit room, being issued pinned ink. Gideon gave him a full bottle off the Survey's stores, which I've never seen him do for anyone, and talked at him the whole time, chick this and sir that and three bottles of ink and a prayer, so that the man would have something to listen to while he wrote a Form 9 for the swap he had spent forty-nine days avoiding. He was going home at dawn. Unballasted. This time the bill would name what went.
When they'd gone I stayed in Cressida's doorway.
"Chief. My name. The thirty days."
"How many days is it?"
"Twelve."
"Then it's eighteen days from relevant." She didn't look up. "Thirty days. Ask me again when it's relevant."

Filing a case means walking the card down the Far Map gallery to the case drawer at the end. The gallery is long. The dead-pin board takes up the whole of the end wall: every pinned branch whose doors have stopped opening, a red pin each, with the year's count chalked underneath.
I had walked past it every day since I joined the Survey. That night I stopped and read it, because I was grounded and had nowhere to be.
Footnote: when I'm frightened I make lists. I didn't know yet that I was frightened.
One. Last year's column: six red pins. This year's: twelve, and the year isn't done.
Two. Every one of them is past distance twenty. Not one is on the Near Map.
Three. Every card is stamped the same: natural decay.
Four. Lowbridge, on the live board across the gallery, is distance twenty-three.
I filed the Teague case under rent, closed the drawer, and went home. My mother called me Edric on the stairs. I answered.

At dawn on day thirteen we walked Amos Teague to the Ninefold's north door. Cressida, Brisk, Verity at her arm's length from the frame, me, and Josiah, who had asked to come and whom nobody had the heart to refuse.

The north door is oak, iron-studded, older than the Hall's own roof. Amos stood in it with his bill folded in his breast pocket. He looked at Josiah once. Josiah nodded at him. Neither of them knew what else to do with the other.
Amos read the route. Twenty-three hinges, in order, in a clear archivist's voice that did not shake.
Brisk had her breath ready to count. She didn't get to nine.
Nothing opened. The door stayed a door. Through it, the cold back corridor of our own Hall.
"Again," said Brisk.
Cressida stepped up herself, because her licence reaches Lowbridge and Brisk's doesn't, and read it in her flat clean voice, every hinge.
Nothing.
Doors don't misdeliver, and they don't sulk. Two readers. One route. Nothing.
Cressida took the Lowbridge card out of her coat and looked at it the way she'd looked at the rent line. "Ardent," she said. "Find me a red pin."

Amos Teague stood in a doorway to nowhere with a bill in his pocket for a swap that would never come. He had no native branch now. He couldn't make ballast. Every branch in the Fan would charge him rent, starting with the one he was standing in.
He was the Bole's first refugee. At midnight, and every seventh midnight after, his rent would land on Josiah Teague of Tallow Street, charged to a door that no longer opened onto anything.
